title: What to Do When Your Asynchronous Video Lessons Aren't Great But You've Got to Post Them e-got-to-post-them-before-you-go-crazy
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing in August 2020, Dave Stuart Jr. argues that teachers publishing asynchronous instructional videos should adopt a firm rule: never re-record them, even when the results are imperfect. He illustrates the temptation toward perfectionism with a personal story about rushing to film a motivation mini-course and cringing at his own mistakes afterward, then explains why distance learning's asynchronous format makes perfectionism an especially dangerous trap compared to the natural time constraints of in-person teaching. Drawing on Sull and Eisenhardt's concept of simple rules, he proposes "we don't reshoot" as a boundary that keeps video production sustainable rather than paralyzing. The piece closes with several practical truths from his own experience of publishing "annoying" videos anyway, framing imperfection as something that can build teacher credibility rather than undermine it.
points: Stuart's core rule of thumb: never re-record asynchronous instructional videos, because reshooting isn't sustainable given teachers' time constraints.
He draws on Sull and Eisenhardt's "simple rules" concept, arguing that a clear boundary reduces overthinking and decision fatigue under pressure.
Distance learning's asynchronous format is a uniquely risky trap for perfectionism because students can replay mistakes repeatedly, unlike a single in-person class period.
Visible imperfection, paired with a colleague check-in for "a glow and a grow," can actually strengthen a teacher's credibility rather than damage it.
quotes: In fact, I'll explain in this article why the rule of thumb we need to aim for is never re-recording our asynchronous instructional videos even though this certainly means we'll be publishing work that is beneath our best sometimes.

In some videos, I hear myself rambling; in others, I clearly misspeak; in one, there's a silly editing mistake at the end. Now in hindsight when I look at the videos as a set, I disagree with how I've organized the content.

As Doug Fisher (co-author on the Distance Learning Playbook) recently made clear to me during a workshop he was leading, in-person instructional models are rooted in time in a way that distance learning is not.
Years ago, Donald Sull and Kathleen Eisenhardt provided a fundamental insight for my work and my life: you can often solve complexity through the use of simple rules.

No fancy editing. I do a little audio tweaking and intro/outro stuff on my videos for teachers, but never for my videos for students. This isn't because I don't love my students; it's because I love having a life.
The awkwardness shows our humanity, and students appreciate it. Paradoxically, it will increase our credibility, not decrease it.
